Stochastic differential equation for the evolution of the global mean temperature: the thermal inertia times the change of temperature equals the net energy flux, that is the short-wave solar radiation absorbed by the Earth after reflection by the temperature-dependent albedo, plus the trapping of outgoing radiation by greenhouse gases and the logarithmic forcing by the CO2 concentration relative to its preindustrial level, minus the outgoing long-wave radiation modified by the emissivity, plus a stochastic forcing by a Wiener process that represents unresolved subgrid processes.

Stochastic delay differential equation for the evolution of the atmospheric CO2 concentration: its change is the emission into the atmosphere, proportional to the current concentration with a time-dependent emission rate, minus the capture of CO2 from the atmosphere by natural processes or technologies, proportional to the concentration one delay earlier with a constant carbon capture rate, plus a stochastic forcing by a Wiener process that represents the uncertainties of the concentration.

Initial condition of the stochastic energy balance equation: at the initial time the global mean temperature equals the given initial global mean temperature, the current global mean temperature in the simulations.

Initial condition of the stochastic delay differential equation for the CO2 concentration: as the equation refers to the concentration one delay earlier, the concentration must be given over the whole delay interval before the initial time, not only at the initial time. It is assumed to be constant over this interval and equal to the initial CO2 concentration, the current level in the simulations.

Delay differential equation for the evolution of the atmospheric CO2 concentration, obtained from the stochastic delay differential equation by neglecting the stochastic term: the change of the concentration is the emission into the atmosphere, proportional to the current concentration with a time-dependent emission rate, minus the capture of CO2, proportional to the concentration one delay earlier with a constant carbon capture rate. Without the noise, it allows an upper bound for the CO2 concentration to be derived analytically, which determines whether an emission reduction and carbon capture scenario keeps the concentration below the critical threshold of the climate tipping point; the noise only adds small fluctuations around this bound.

Assumption that the noise intensity of the atmospheric CO2 concentration is zero, so that its stochastic delay differential equation becomes deterministic; justified as the noise only adds small fluctuations around the deterministic evolution.

Mathematical model for the global mean surface temperature and the atmospheric CO2 concentration, introduced to study climate tipping points under emission reduction and carbon capture scenarios. The temperature follows a Budyko–Sellers-type energy balance: incoming short-wave radiation with a temperature-dependent albedo (a smooth transition between an ice-covered and an ice-free value), greenhouse forcing, and outgoing long-wave radiation, driven by additive white noise. The CO2 concentration follows a stochastic delay differential equation with a time-dependent emission rate as source, a constant carbon capture rate acting with a time delay as sink, and additive white noise. The coupling is one-way: CO2 drives temperature through the greenhouse forcing.

Global albedo of the Earth that depends on the global mean temperature through the melting of ice: it changes smoothly from the current global albedo at low temperatures to the terminal global albedo at high temperatures, between the lower and the upper albedo transition temperature. The decrease of the albedo with rising temperature is the ice–albedo feedback, which causes the tipping point of the model.

Relative rate at which CO2 is emitted into the atmosphere, as a function of time, describing an emission reduction scenario in three periods: a period of inaction in which the rate stays at its current value, a reduction period in which it decreases linearly, and a terminal period in which it stays at its terminal value.

Weight of the terminal global albedo in the temperature-dependent global albedo: it rises from 0 below the lower to 1 above the upper albedo transition temperature, linearly in between, so that the albedo changes from its current to its terminal value as the ice melts. The switches at the two transition temperatures use a smooth approximation of the Heaviside step function by the hyperbolic tangent, whose sharpness is set by the albedo transition rate temperature.

Numerical solution of the initial value problem for the coupled stochastic delay differential equations of the global mean temperature and the atmospheric CO2 concentration. Starting from the current global mean temperature and CO2 concentration, with a constant CO2 history over the preceding delay interval, the system is simulated over a long time span for a range of emission reduction scenarios, given by the terminal emission rate and the time to reach it, to determine whether the CO2 concentration exceeds the critical threshold beyond which the temperature tips into the warm regime.
